derivations.claim: Put $\langle z\rangle=(1+|z|^2)^{1/2}$. The triangle inequality gives $\langle v+w\rangle^r\le C_r\langle v\rangle^r\langle w\rangle^{|r|}$ for every real $r$, also when $r<0$ by interchanging $v$ and $v+w$. For an output-compact symbol $p$ of order $m$, integration by parts in $x$ gives $|\widehat p_x(\zeta,\xi)|\le C_N\langle\zeta\rangle^{-2N}\langle\xi\rangle^m$. Fourier transformation turns its quantization into the kernel $(2\pi)^{-n}\widehat p_x(\eta-\xi,\xi)$. After conjugation by Sobolev weights this is bounded by $C_{N,s}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-2N+|s-m|}$. Choose $2N>n+|s-m|$. Both integrals of this bound, in $\eta$ and in $\xi$, are finite. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by integration in the other variable, bounds the squared operator norm by the product of these two integral bounds. Plancherel proves $H^s\to H^{s-m}$ boundedness and continuity in finitely many output-derivative symbol bounds. This also applies to differences of symbols. No frequency-derivative bound is needed for this particular estimate.

An amplitude $a(x,y,\xi)$, compactly supported in $(x,y)$ and satisfying the symbol bounds of order $m$ with derivatives in both variables, has a quantization with kernel $(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi}a(x,y,\xi)d\xi$, interpreted distributionally. It equals a left quantization with symbol $r(x,\xi)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\zeta}\widehat a_y(x,\zeta,\xi+\zeta)d\zeta$. The latter integral and all its derivatives converge: integration by parts in $y$ gives arbitrary decay in $\zeta$, and the weight inequality in step 1.1 absorbs the frequency shift. Fourier inversion on Schwartz test inputs proves the identity by Fubini; hence it defines the distributional kernel without an unregularized oscillatory exchange. Taylor expansion in the last variable gives $r\sim\sum_\alpha i^{-|\alpha|}(\partial_\xi^\alpha\partial_y^\alpha a)(x,x,\xi)/\alpha!$. Indeed the integral remainder after degree $N-1$ contains $\partial_\xi^\alpha\widehat a_y(x,\zeta,\xi+t\zeta)\zeta^\alpha$, $|\alpha|=N$, integrated against $N(1-t)^{N-1}/\alpha!$; integration by parts in $y$ and the same weight inequality bound every differentiated remainder by $C\langle\xi\rangle^{m-N-|\beta|}$. Thus it is a symbol of order $m-N$, with continuous seminorm estimates. In particular the leading symbol is $a(x,x,\xi)$.

The kernel of a symbol is smooth off $x=y$. On a compact set separated from that diagonal, repeatedly use $e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi}=|x-y|^{-2} (x-y)\cdot(\partial_\xi/i)e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi}$. Each transfer to the symbol lowers its order; after more than $m+n$ transfers the integral is absolutely convergent. To differentiate the kernel a prescribed number of times, transfer that many additional derivatives first. The resulting integrals give continuous derivatives by integrable majorants, and coincide as distributions by testing against Schwartz functions and integration by parts. Thus cutting off a kernel near the diagonal changes it by a smooth kernel. This also justifies arbitrary nested compact chart localizations.

For a coordinate change $z=\kappa(x)$, near the diagonal write $\kappa(x)-\kappa(y)=H(x,y)(x-y)$ with $H(x,y)=\int_0^1d\kappa_{y+t(x-y)}dt$. Shrink the coordinate neighborhood so that $H$ is invertible, and change frequency by $\eta=H(x,y)^t\xi$. The transformed kernel is an amplitude of order $m$: differentiating $p(\kappa(x),H^{-t}\eta)$ introduces a frequency derivative together with at most one factor of $\eta$, preserving its order. Smooth frame and density factors have bounded derivatives. At $x=y$, the Jacobian $|\det d\kappa_y|$ from the source density cancels $|\det H|^{-1}$. Step 2.1 therefore gives exactly the cotangent transformation of $p_m$; all other terms have order $m-1$. Cover the compact diagonal by finitely many such neighborhoods and use step 2.2 off it. This proves covariance, including continuous parameter-dependent coordinate changes on compact parameter subsets. The ordinary chain rule, change of variables and the weight inequality prove equivalence of the integer positive Sobolev norms; negative norms follow by duality, and the Fourier completion defines the corresponding distribution spaces.

For two output-compact left symbols $p,q$, Fourier inversion gives the composition symbol $r(x,\xi)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\zeta}p(x,\xi+\zeta)\widehat q_x(\zeta,\xi)d\zeta$. Arbitrary decay of $\widehat q_x$ and step 1.1 justify the integral with every derivative. Taylor expansion of $p$ gives $r\sim\sum_\alpha i^{-|\alpha|}(\partial_\xi^\alpha p)(\partial_x^\alpha q)/\alpha!$; the explicit integral remainder is bounded exactly as in step 2.1, now by $C\langle\xi\rangle^{m+m'-N-|\beta|}$. The adjoint kernel has amplitude $p(y,\xi)^*$ with the smooth density and metric factors inserted; its diagonal value is $p_m(x,\xi)^*$. Steps 2.1–3.1 prove the adjoint assertion, and yield $\Psi^m\Psi^{m'}\subset\Psi^{m+m'}$. Partitions realize any homogeneous symbol: multiply it by a high-frequency cutoff, quantize in charts, and sum with cutoffs whose squares sum to one. The diagonal symbol is the given bundle map. The same construction is linear and continuous on smooth symbol families.

The symbol expansions just obtained can be summed. For a sequence $b_j\in S^{m-j}$ choose radii $R_j\uparrow\infty$ and a fixed cutoff $\chi$ zero on the unit ball and one outside the ball of radius two. For $j\ge1$, make the first $j$ seminorms of $\chi(\xi/R_j)b_j$ in $S^{m-j+1}$ smaller than $2^{-j}$. This is possible because on its support the extra order gives a factor $R_j^{-1}$, and cutoff derivatives give the compensating inverse powers. For each fixed symbol seminorm and each fixed $N$, the tail starting beyond $N$ converges in $S^{m-N}$; the finite remaining terms cause no difficulty. Thus $b=\sum_j\chi(\xi/R_j)b_j$ has the prescribed expansion. AC permits these countably many choices. If $P$ is elliptic, first quantize $\sigma(P)^{-1}$ with cutoff to obtain $Q_0$ and $I-PQ_0$ of order $-1$. Sum the formal series $Q_0\sum_{k\ge0}(I-PQ_0)^k$ by this construction to obtain a right parametrix modulo all negative orders. A left parametrix is constructed likewise; their difference is smoothing because $Q_L-Q_R=Q_L(I-PQ_R)-(I-Q_LP)Q_R$. An operator of every negative order has a smooth kernel by the absolutely convergent derivative integrals from steps 2.1–2.2. This proves the asserted two-sided smooth remainders.

The Fourier definition implies $\bigcap_sH^s=C^\infty$: if $s>n/2+k$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $|\xi|^k\widehat u$ integrable and Fourier inversion gives continuous derivatives through order $k$. Conversely smooth chart coefficients have arbitrary Fourier decay. Every distribution on a compact chart subset has finite order, and its Fourier transform grows at most polynomially, by testing it on a cutoff times $e^{-ix\cdot\xi}$; hence every distribution on compact $X$ belongs to some $H^{-s}$. The parametrix identity $u=QPu+Ru$ now proves elliptic regularity, including $Pu\in H^s\Rightarrow u\in H^{s+m}$ whenever $u$ is a distribution. Order $-1$ operators send $L^2$ to $H^1$ by step 1.1; [F2] in finitely many balls makes their $L^2$ realizations compact. Applying the same fact to integer Sobolev derivatives and, for negative orders, duality gives compactness of $H^{s+1}\hookrightarrow H^s$. Thus the parametrix remainders are compact on all Sobolev spaces; [F3] proves Fredholmness. Distributional adjoint kernels are smooth, so cokernels are their finite-dimensional smooth kernels. These arguments include dimension one.

Choose real cutoffs $\phi_i$ with $\sum_i\phi_i^2=1$ in finitely many bundle charts. Trivialize unitarily, incorporating the square root of the density into the chart map $T_i$ to make it an $L^2$ isometry on supported sections. Define $\Lambda_E=\sum_i\phi_iT_i^{-1}\langle D\rangle T_i\phi_i$, with zero extension before the Fourier multiplier. It is symmetric on smooth sections and satisfies $(\Lambda_Eu,u)\ge\sum_i\|\phi_i u\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2$. Steps 3.1–4.1 give positive scalar homogeneous symbol $\ell=\sum_i\phi_i^2|\xi|_i$, the same for all bundles if their coordinate cover is shared. Elliptic regularity makes the adjoint kernel smooth; symmetry and the inequality make both kernel and cokernel zero. Hence $\Lambda_E:H^1\to L^2$ is bijective with bounded inverse. The parametrix identities show that this inverse differs from its classical parametrix by a smooth-kernel operator: the difference is $\Lambda_E^{-1}$ times a smooth remainder, which maps every negative Sobolev space to every positive one by elliptic regularity and the bounded inverse; this implies a smooth kernel as follows. After localization, the matrix coefficient between cutoff plane waves of frequencies $\xi,\eta$ is bounded by $C_{a,b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-a}\langle\eta\rangle^{-b}$ for arbitrary $a,b$, using the $H^{-a}\to H^b$ bound and the Schwartz Fourier decay of the cutoffs. It is the double Fourier transform of the localized kernel. Its rapid decay with the same bounds after coordinate multiplication makes inverse Fourier differentiation absolutely convergent to every order, giving a smooth kernel. Integer powers and inverse powers are consequently classical, and give the stated $H^s\leftrightarrow L^2$ identifications for all integers.

For $P\in\Psi^0$, let $p_0=\sigma_0(P)$ on $S^*X$. Its essential norm on $L^2$ is exactly $\|p_0\|_\infty$. For the upper bound fix $c>\|p_0\|_\infty$ and quantize $h_0=(c^2I-p_0^*p_0)^{1/2}$. This is smooth: a uniformly convergent power series for the square root on a slightly larger spectral interval can be differentiated on the compact base, or one may use the convergent resolvent integral for positive matrices. Step 4.1 gives $c^2I-P^*P-H^*H$ compact. A compact operator is uniformly approximated by finite-rank operators: project its relatively compact unit-ball image onto the span of a finite small net. On the common orthogonal complement of the finite-dimensional ranges of an approximant and its adjoint the compact quadratic error is arbitrarily small; hence $\|P(I-\Pi)\|\le(c^2+\varepsilon)^{1/2}$ for a finite-rank projection $\Pi$. Since $P\Pi$ is compact, the essential norm is at most $c$, and then at most $\|p_0\|_\infty$.

For the lower bound choose chart data $(x_0,\xi_0,v)$ with $|\xi_0|=|v|=1$, and a smooth bump $\varphi_\delta$ supported within distance $\delta$ of $x_0$, normalized in $L^2$. Put $u_k=e^{ik\xi_0\cdot x}\varphi_\delta v$. It converges weakly to zero: for smooth test sections integrate by parts in the $\xi_0$ direction, and extend to $L^2$ tests by density. Modulation replaces the local symbol by $p(x,k\xi_0+\eta)$. For every fixed $\eta$, its order-zero bounds and classical expansion give uniform convergence on the compact output support to $p_0(x,\xi_0)$; its norm is bounded uniformly in $k,x,\eta$. Thus the absolutely convergent Fourier integral against the Schwartz function $\widehat\varphi_\delta(\eta)$ converges uniformly in $x$, by first truncating its integrable tail. The output support is fixed, so $\|Pu_k-e^{ik\xi_0\cdot x}p_0(x,\xi_0)\varphi_\delta v\|_2\to0$. Chart cutoffs contribute only smooth kernels by step 2.2, and those kernels send this weakly zero sequence to zero. Every compact operator does likewise, because any convergent subsequence of its images has weak limit zero. Therefore the essential norm is at least $\|p_0(x,\xi_0)\varphi_\delta v\|_2$. Send $\delta\downarrow0$, then take the supremum over the data, to obtain the reverse inequality to step 7.2. For zero-dimensional $X$, the sphere is empty and every operator is compact.

Smooth kernels include finite-rank operators with smooth vectors, which are norm dense in all compact operators by smooth density and the finite-net argument in step 7.2. The essential-norm identity extends the principal symbol continuously to the norm closure, with kernel exactly the compact operators. It is onto the continuous symbols: choose smooth approximants $a_j$ whose successive uniform differences are less than $2^{-j}$. Quantize each difference. The essential-norm upper bound allows subtraction of a compact operator so that the adjusted lift has norm at most $2\|a_{j+1}-a_j\|_\infty$; compact operators already lie in the closure. The adjusted lifts form a norm-convergent series realizing the continuous limit. Continuous sections admit the required smooth approximation by finite local convolutions and partitions, with ordinary matrix bundle transitions. Conjugate an order-$m$ realization by $\Lambda_F^{s-m}$ on the left and $\Lambda_E^{-s}$ on the right. Step 7.1 turns it into an order-zero operator with symbol $p_m\ell^{-m}$. This transports the exact sequence to every pair $(m,s)$.

Average positive densities and bundle metrics using [F4]; their averages are smooth and positive by differentiation of their local smooth expressions over the compact parameter group. With these choices $U_g$ is unitary on $L^2$ and uniformly bounded on every Sobolev space by the chart chain-rule bounds. Step 3.1, including its amplitude remainder estimates, shows that conjugation of a fixed classical operator varies continuously in each classical seminorm as $g$ varies: use finitely many group neighborhoods and source-target charts, whose transition amplitudes and all derivatives depend smoothly on $g$. The off-diagonal kernels have the same property by step 2.2. Consequently the Haar integral exists in every symbol seminorm, and differentiation under its uniformly bounded local amplitudes makes it classical with averaged leading symbol. Averaging the operator $\Lambda_E$ constructed in step 7.1 therefore preserves its positivity, ellipticity and scalar leading symbol, making a common invariant $\ell$ available. Approximation extends operator averaging to each operator-norm closure and the simultaneous closure; uniform boundedness of the conjugations at each Sobolev level passes continuity from classical approximants to their limit, and invariance of the average follows by changing the group integration variable. In particular, a lift from step 9.1 of an invariant continuous inverse symbol can be averaged in the single-level closure and retains that inverse symbol. Smooth paths are norm continuous by step 1.1 and the finite chart construction. This construction uses no Fredholmness or regularity assertion for the closures.

In the closure at one Sobolev level, an invertible continuous symbol has a lift of its inverse by step 9.1. Compositions differ from the identity by compact operators, so [F3] gives Fredholmness. An operator in the simultaneous closure has this property at every level when its symbol is invertible. Its index is independent of the level: approximate it simultaneously at two chosen levels and uniformly in symbol by a classical operator with invertible symbol. Averaging a classical approximant as in step 10.1 preserves classicality and its averaged symbol; sufficiently close approximation keeps that symbol invertible. For an equivariant Fredholm operator $P:H\to H'$, use the invariant decompositions $H=\ker P\oplus(\ker P)^\perp$ and $H'=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp\oplus\operatorname{ran}P$. The restriction from $(\ker P)^\perp$ to $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a bounded equivariant isomorphism. For every sufficiently close equivariant $Q$, its infinite block between these two subspaces remains invertible by the Neumann series. Equivariant invertible row and column operations reduce $Q$ to that block and a map $S:\ker P\to(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$. Invariant orthogonal splitting of $\ker S$ and $\operatorname{ran}S$ gives $[\ker Q]-[\operatorname{coker}Q]=[\ker S]-[\operatorname{coker}S]=[\ker P]-[\operatorname{coker}P]$ in $R(G)$. Thus the virtual index is locally constant at either Sobolev level. For the classical approximant, elliptic regularity identifies its kernels and adjoint kernels at both levels, so their $R(G)$-indices agree; local constancy then gives the same index for the original closure operator.

Since $\ker P:H^{s+1}\to H^{s+1-m}$ is contained in the kernel at level $s$, its dimension can only decrease as $s$ increases. The cokernel is the kernel of the distributional formal adjoint in $H^{m-s}$; its dimension can only increase. Constancy of their difference from step 11.1 forces both dimensions, and therefore both kernel spaces, to be constant. Membership in every Sobolev space gives smoothness by step 6.1. If $Pu=f$ with $f$ smooth, then at every higher level $f$ is orthogonal to exactly the same smooth adjoint kernel, so closed range gives a preimage $u_s$ at that level. The difference $u-u_s$ lies in the already smooth distributional kernel. Hence $u$ belongs to every Sobolev space and is smooth. This also proves the asserted regularity for the simultaneous closure without assuming that its inverse is classical. On a compact zero-manifold all spaces are finite direct sums, the sphere symbols are empty, and all assertions reduce to finite-dimensional linear algebra; the empty manifold gives zero spaces. This proves every assertion.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, put $n=\dim X$, and fix a smooth Riemannian metric, a positive density, and Hermitian metrics on smooth finite-rank complex bundles $E,F\to X$. Let $\pi:T^*X\to X$ be the bundle projection, use the dual metric to define $|\xi|$ and $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$, and use the induced operator norm for local symbol matrices. In a coordinate chart and local bundle frames, a symbol of integer order $m$ is a smooth matrix $p(x,\xi)$ satisfying, on each compact coordinate subset,

$$|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\langle\xi\rangle^{m-|\beta|}.$$

A classical symbol also has homogeneous terms $p_{m-j}(x,\xi)$, smooth for $\xi\ne0$, such that subtracting the first $N$ terms, multiplied by a cutoff zero near $\xi=0$ and one for large $\xi$, gives a symbol of order $m-N$. Quantization means

$$\operatorname{Op}(p)u(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}p(x,\xi)\widehat u(\xi)\,d\xi,\qquad\widehat u(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx,$$

localized by smooth cutoffs in source and target. Define $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ to be operators given by finite sums of these local classical quantizations and operators with smooth kernels. Define integer Sobolev spaces by finite-chart Fourier norms $\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat u\|_2$, using distributions for negative $s$; different finite-chart choices give equivalent norms.

This class is independent of charts and frames. Its leading symbol is a well-defined smooth homogeneous bundle map $\sigma_m(P):\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, satisfying $\sigma_m(P)(x,t\xi)=t^m\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. Every such map is realized. Call $P$ elliptic when $\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $(x,\xi)$ with $\xi\ne0$. A two-sided parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ is an operator $Q\in\Psi^{-m}(X;F,E)$ such that $QP-I_E$ and $PQ-I_F$ are operators with smooth Schwartz kernels. A Fredholm realization at Sobolev level $s$ is the bounded map $P:H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range, and finite-dimensional cokernel $H^{s-m}(F)/\operatorname{ran}P$; in the Hilbert structures above its cokernel is represented by the kernel of the Hilbert adjoint. Composition and formal adjoint have leading symbols $\sigma(PQ)=\sigma(P)\sigma(Q)$ and $\sigma(P^*)=\sigma(P)^*$; zero leading symbol lowers the order by one. Every $P\in\Psi^m$ extends boundedly $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$, continuously in the symbol seminorms. Negative-order operators are compact on $L^2$. For elliptic $P$, the two-sided parametrix just defined yields Fredholm realizations at every integer $s$ and distributional elliptic regularity: $Pu\in C^\infty$ implies $u\in C^\infty$.

There is a positive invertible elliptic order-one operator $\Lambda_E$ on each bundle. Here positive means formally symmetric and $\langle\Lambda_Eu,u\rangle_{L^2(E)}\ge\|u\|_{L^2(E)}^2$ for every smooth section $u$; its closed realization on $L^2(E)$ has domain $H^1(E)$, and $\Lambda_E:H^1(E)\to L^2(E)$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse. Its positive scalar leading symbol $\ell(x,\xi)$ is chosen the same for all bundles over $X$. The distributional extensions $\Lambda_E:H^r(E)\to H^{r-1}(E)$ are isomorphisms for every integer $r$; $\Lambda_E^s:H^s(E)\to L^2(E)$ denotes the $s$-fold iterate when $s>0$, the inverse iterate when $s<0$, and the identity when $s=0$. In these equivalent norms the operator-norm closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ acting as $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ has a continuous surjective normalized symbol map to $C(S^*X;\operatorname{Hom}(\pi^*E,\pi^*F))$, with kernel exactly the compact operators; normalization divides the homogeneous symbol by $\ell^m$. Here $S^*X=\{(x,\xi)\in T^*X:|\xi|=1\}$.

Let $\overline\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ denote the closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ in all the seminorms $\|P\|_{H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)}$, $s\in\mathbb Z$. Its leading homogeneous symbol is continuous, and invertibility gives Fredholmness at every level and smooth kernels and adjoint kernels. The kernels are independent of $s$, and smooth data in the range have smooth preimages. Smooth symbol paths admit norm-continuous quantizations; a path continuous in the classical symbol seminorms is continuous at every indicated operator norm.

If a compact Lie group $G$ acts smoothly on $X,E,F$, write $\rho_g(y):E_y\to E_{gy}$ for its bundle action and set $(U_gu)(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, with the analogous action on $F$. Invariant density and metrics can be chosen. Conjugation $P\mapsto U_gPU_g^{-1}$ is continuous in the classical symbol seminorms and in the displayed closures. Haar averaging commutes with the symbol map and preserves these classes, orders and smooth kernels. All assertions therefore apply to $G$-invariant operators, including $G=T\times O(k)$.

derivations.claim: The elementary change used below is the following bundle rotation. For two isomorphic summands, the matrix $R_\theta=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is invertible with inverse $R_{-\theta}$. If their identification is an invertible map $h:A\to B$, its expression on $A\oplus B$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta h^{-1}\\\sin\theta h&\cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The formula is used only where $h$ is invertible, and can be joined to the identity using a scalar cutoff $\theta$ supported in that region. Applying the corresponding rotations to source and target commutes with a diagonal map $h\oplus I$. Invariant scalar cutoffs exist by averaging ordinary smooth cutoffs over the compact group.

On a compact invariant base, a continuous equivariant bundle embeds in a trivial finite-dimensional representation bundle. Choose finitely many continuous local generators, extended by cutoffs, whose evaluations span every fiber. Average a continuous nonnegative bump on $G$, of integral one and supported near its identity, against the translates of each section; the resulting section is uniformly close to it. Approximate this bump uniformly by a representative function using [F3]. The resulting averaged sections are still uniformly close and each belongs to a finite-dimensional translation-invariant space, since the left translates of its coefficient function span such a space. Surjectivity of a finite family of fiber evaluations is stable under a sufficiently small uniform perturbation, by a positive minimum singular value on the compact base. Their finite orbit spans therefore give an equivariant surjection $V\times Z\to A$. Haar-average the bundle metric; its adjoint embeds $A$ equivariantly in $V\times Z$, and the orthogonal image projection is continuous. This proof also works on a neighborhood of a compact invariant subset, and for a bundle trivial outside a compact subset, retaining the finite exterior generators.

Realize a smooth $c$ by [F1] and Haar-average the realization, giving an invariant elliptic operator $P$. Two realizations with the same symbol differ by a compact operator on the relevant Sobolev spaces. A path of invariant Fredholm operators has constant virtual index: split domain as $\ker P\oplus(\ker P)^\perp$ and target as $\operatorname{ran}P\oplus(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$. Nearby operators have an invertible infinite block by a Neumann series. Invertible equivariant triangular row and column operations reduce them to that block and a map $S$ between the fixed finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel spaces. Invariant orthogonal splitting of $S$ gives $[\ker S]-[\operatorname{coker}S]=[\ker P]-[\operatorname{coker}P]$. This proves local constancy in $R(G)$, hence constancy along a continuous path. In particular compact perturbations preserve it, since the whole compact-perturbation path is Fredholm by [F1]. The same argument applies to homogeneous symbols of any order and their simultaneous-closure realizations, using [F1] at one Sobolev level.

A finite-dimensional continuous representation of a compact Lie group is smooth in the needed matrix coordinates. Indeed choose a smooth bump $h$ near the identity so that $C=\int h(g)\rho(g)dg$ is invertible. Then $\rho(k)C=\int h(k^{-1}g)\rho(g)dg$ is smooth in $k$, by differentiating the smooth bump on the compact group; multiplication by $C^{-1}$ proves the assertion. For a continuous equivariant orthogonal projection $p:Z\to\operatorname{End}(V)$ over a compact smooth base, approximate its entries uniformly by smooth functions in local charts and patch with a partition; symmetrize and average over $G$. The smooth equivariant selfadjoint result $q$ can be made arbitrarily close to $p$. If $\|q-p\|<1/4$, the contour projection $p'= (2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z-1|=1/2}(z-q)^{-1}dz$ is smooth and equivariant, has the same rank, and is arbitrarily close to $p$ as the approximation improves. The restriction $p'|_{\operatorname{im}p}$ is an isomorphism when $\|p'-p\|<1$, proving that the original bundle is equivariantly isomorphic to a smooth one. The resolvent identity gives the claimed closeness; the spectral projection and its rank follow by diagonalizing the finite selfadjoint matrix and integrating $(z-\lambda)^{-1}$ around the circle. Apply the same construction to a homotopy on a compact base times an interval, with approximation relative to smooth endpoints by using a parameter cutoff. Small perturbations of a bundle map preserve invertibility on any fixed compact set where its least singular value is positive.

Here is the precise compact-local replacement, including the stabilization needed to change the exterior bundles. Write $Z=T^*X$ or $T^*U$, and choose invariant relatively compact open sets $O_1\Subset O_2\subset Z$ containing the support, so $b$ is invertible on $Z\setminus\overline O_1$. By step 1.2 choose a finite representation $V$ and a complement $H$ to $B$ over a neighborhood of $\overline O_2$, identifying $B\oplus H$ with $V$ there. Glue $A\oplus H$ on $O_2$ to the trivial $V$-bundle outside $\overline O_1$ by $b\oplus I_H$ on their overlap. Call this bundle $A'$, and let $c:A'\to V$ be $b\oplus I_H$ inside and the identity outside. The triple $(A',V,c)$ has trivial exterior bundles. It is stably isomorphic to the original triple: compare $(A\oplus V,B\oplus V,b\oplus I_V)$ with $(A'\oplus B,V\oplus B,c\oplus I_B)$. Inside $O_2$, write $v=v_B+h$ in $V=B\oplus H$. At $\theta=0$ identify the source by $(a,v)\mapsto((a,-h),v_B)$ and the target by $(z,v)\mapsto((z,-h),v_B)$. In the annulus rotate the two $B$ coordinates $(ba,v_B)$ in the source and $(z,v_B)$ in the target through a cutoff angle from zero to $\pi/2$, keeping the $H$ coordinate $-h$. Step 1.1 makes these invertible identifications and makes the triple maps commute. At $\theta=\pi/2$, the gluing identifies the source map with $(a,v)\mapsto(-v,ba)$ and the target map with $(z,v)\mapsto(-v,z)$, both defined throughout the exterior without any complement there. Thus the identifications glue globally and the two stabilized triples are isomorphic. No exterior bundle was presumed extendible. The same construction proves locality under changing the exterior space. The new bundles are trivial outside a compact set, so step 1.2 gives global finite representation embeddings; their exterior evaluation maps, and hence their projections, may be held constant. Step 2.1 then smooths them and the map relative to that exterior. All choices are uniform over a compact homotopy parameter. This proves reduction of continuous compact-support triples to smooth ones without a prior smooth structure on their original bundles.

Choose smooth connections by patching the chart connections with a partition and Haar-average them. Parallel transport along $t\mapsto(x,t\xi)$ identifies a smooth equivariant bundle over $T^*X$ with the pullback of its zero-section bundle. The linear transport ODE on each compact segment has a unique invertible solution, depends smoothly on its parameters, and preserves equivariance because the averaged connection and the radial paths do. One may obtain this solution directly by the convergent iterated-integral series in each finite chart segment; on a compact segment its $k$th term is bounded by $C^k/k!$, and differentiated series on compact parameter sets converge after increasing $C$. This also proves independence of subdivisions and the parameter-homotopy assertion. For a noncompact $U$ with controlled exterior data, choose the connection to be the trivial one there before averaging, so the radial identification is the identity off the same compact base subset.

In these pullback identifications choose $R$ so large that $b$ is invertible for $|\xi|\ge R$ over the compact base region in question. Compose $b$ with a radial map which is the identity for $|\xi|\le R$, has radius $2R$ for $|\xi|\ge2R$, and keeps radii at least $R$ for $|\xi|\ge R$. Interpolation between its radius and $|\xi|$ is an admissible homotopy, because the whole exterior remains invertible. The resulting exterior is the homogeneous degree-zero invertible map $c(x,\xi)=b(x,2R\xi/|\xi|)$. Replace the interior by any cutoff extension of $c$; interpolate linearly inside the disk, holding the exterior fixed. Noninvertibility is allowed there, so this is another admissible homotopy. Smooth approximation of a continuous $c$ on the compact sphere bundle, followed by averaging, preserves invertibility and gives a path through invertible sphere symbols; its least singular value has a positive minimum. Exterior identity data can be kept fixed throughout. These operations prove homogeneous presentation, also for homotopies.

Quantization of a smooth symbol homotopy is norm continuous by [F1]. Continuous homotopies were reduced to such paths in steps 2.1–5.1. For bundles varying with the parameter, embed into a common representation over the compact parameter space as in step 1.2. Their projection matrices vary uniformly continuously; subdivide the interval until successive projections are less than one apart, so projection restriction identifies successive fibers invertibly. For smooth projections the connection transport of step 4.1 gives the same endpoint identifications through a smooth family. Thus the index is independent of smoothing, complements, radial choices and homotopies. Block sums give sums of kernels and cokernels. An everywhere-invertible triple can be kept invertible during radial collapse to its zero-section map, giving a base bundle isomorphism; multiplication by that isomorphism has index zero. Isomorphic triples give conjugate kernels. These facts prove that elementary stabilizations and every comparison in the Statement preserve the index. Changing the order multiplies the symbol by a positive scalar power of the elliptic $\Lambda$ in [F1], whose realization is an isomorphism and has zero index.

For the noncompact statement the compression in step 3.1, followed by radial transport, makes $E,F$ the common trivial representation bundle outside a compact base subset, and $c$ equals its identity there. Extend both bundles to the supplied compact ambient by those exterior trivializations, and use [F1] to choose any invariant realization $P_0$ of $c$. Choose invariant smooth cutoffs $\eta_1,\eta_2$ compactly supported in $U$, with $\eta_1=1$ on a neighborhood of the base subset and $\eta_2=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\eta_1$. Let $h:E\to F$ be the exterior identity, defined wherever $1-\eta_1$ is nonzero, and set $P=\eta_2P_0\eta_1+h(1-\eta_1)$. The last term is extended by zero where its multiplier vanishes. Its principal symbol is $\eta_2\eta_1c+(1-\eta_1)h=c$: where the first cutoff is not one, $c=h$, and where it is nonzero the second cutoff is one. The nonlocal part of the kernel is supported in $L\times L$, $L=\operatorname{supp}\eta_2$; the remaining term is multiplication by the exterior identity. In particular outside $L$, in either the source or target variable, $P$ is precisely that identity. Thus no global isomorphism between the possibly different interior bundles $E,F$ is asserted. Averaging preserves this control since the cutoffs and exterior data are invariant.

Conjugation by an equivariant diffeomorphism transports every operator and its kernels. Restricting the group action changes neither operator nor vector spaces; any already invariant realization remains a valid realization after restriction. Tensoring by a finite-dimensional representation tensors kernels and adjoint kernels, since the operator acts as $P\otimes I$. On a point an arbitrary linear equivariant map has virtual kernel-minus-cokernel equal to domain-minus-target by finite-dimensional orthogonal splitting. These establish the stated naturality and coefficient assertions without imposing any Bott normalization.

Let $d$ be a first-order elliptic differential complex and put $D=d+d^*$. At nonzero $\xi$, write $a=\sigma(d)$; then $a^2=0$ and exactness implies $a+a^*$ is invertible, since its squared norm on $v$ is $\|av\|^2+\|a^*v\|^2$ and exactness gives $\ker a\cap\ker a^*=\{0\}$. Thus the Hodge operators $\Delta_j$ and $D$ have elliptic realizations by [F1], even when their principal symbols are matrices. For $\Delta_j$, symmetry identifies its cokernel with its smooth kernel; the Fredholm range is their orthogonal complement. Its inverse on that complement is bounded from $L^2$ to $H^2$ by [F4] and the elliptic estimate, which follows from a parametrix. Denote this inverse by $G_j$, zero on the harmonic kernel, and its projection by $\Pi_j$. The differential commutes with $\Delta$ on smooth sections. Harmonic sections are killed by both $d$ and $d^*$ by the nonnegative squared-norm identity. Hence $dG u$ and $Gdu$ are both orthogonal to harmonic sections and solve the same equation with source $du$; uniqueness gives $dG=Gd$ on smooth sections, and gives $I-\Pi=dd^*G+d^*dG$. A closed smooth section therefore equals its harmonic projection plus $d(d^*G u)$. Exact harmonic sections vanish by integration by parts. This proves unique harmonic representatives, finite-dimensional cohomology, and $\ker D^+=\bigoplus_{j\,\mathrm{even}}\ker\Delta_j$, $\ker(D^+)^*=\bigoplus_{j\,\mathrm{odd}}\ker\Delta_j$. To check the symbol-class identification explicitly, exactness gives the orthogonal bundle decompositions $E^j=\operatorname{im}a_{j-1}\oplus\operatorname{im}a_j^*$ over the nonzero cotangent vectors; each restriction $a_j:\operatorname{im}a_j^*\to\operatorname{im}a_j$ is an equivariant bundle isomorphism. In the even-to-odd block of $a+a^*$, these isomorphisms and their adjoints occur once each, after only permuting the image summands. Hence the folded block represents the compactly supported symbol class of the exact complex, not merely an operator with the same numerical index. The Hodge kernel calculation above then makes its analytic index the alternating cohomology representation. All operations commute with $G$ and apply in particular to de Rham forms.

Extend this controlled operator to either compact ambient. Outside $L$ its equation is $u=0$, so its smooth kernel consists exactly of solutions on $U$ supported in $L$. Such a solution extends smoothly by zero, since $L$ is compactly contained in $U$. Restriction and zero extension therefore identify the two ambient kernel representations. The adjoint has the same support property, because its nonidentity kernel is obtained by transposing a kernel supported in $L\times L$. The adjoint kernels, and hence cokernel representations by [F1], are likewise identical. This proves ambient independence and excision. All choices and triple comparisons have already been shown to preserve the index, so this controlled calculation computes the originally given compact-support data rather than just one preferred representative. Empty manifolds, zero bundles and rank-zero symbols give zero spaces; compact zero-manifolds give finite direct sums of the point calculation in step 7.1. This completes the proof.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, put $n=\dim X$, and fix a smooth Riemannian metric, a positive density, and Hermitian metrics on smooth finite-rank complex bundles $E,F\to X$. Let $\pi:T^*X\to X$ be the bundle projection, use the dual metric to define $|\xi|$ and $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$, and use the induced operator norm for local symbol matrices. In a coordinate chart and local bundle frames, a symbol of integer order $m$ is a smooth matrix $p(x,\xi)$ satisfying, on each compact coordinate subset,

$$|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\langle\xi\rangle^{m-|\beta|}.$$

A classical symbol also has homogeneous terms $p_{m-j}(x,\xi)$, smooth for $\xi\ne0$, such that subtracting the first $N$ terms, multiplied by a cutoff zero near $\xi=0$ and one for large $\xi$, gives a symbol of order $m-N$. Quantization means

$$\operatorname{Op}(p)u(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}p(x,\xi)\widehat u(\xi)\,d\xi,\qquad\widehat u(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx,$$

localized by smooth cutoffs in source and target. Define $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ to be operators given by finite sums of these local classical quantizations and operators with smooth kernels. Define integer Sobolev spaces by finite-chart Fourier norms $\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat u\|_2$, using distributions for negative $s$; different finite-chart choices give equivalent norms.

This class is independent of charts and frames. Its leading symbol is a well-defined smooth homogeneous bundle map $\sigma_m(P):\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, satisfying $\sigma_m(P)(x,t\xi)=t^m\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. Every such map is realized. Call $P$ elliptic when $\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $(x,\xi)$ with $\xi\ne0$. A two-sided parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ is an operator $Q\in\Psi^{-m}(X;F,E)$ such that $QP-I_E$ and $PQ-I_F$ are operators with smooth Schwartz kernels. A Fredholm realization at Sobolev level $s$ is the bounded map $P:H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range, and finite-dimensional cokernel $H^{s-m}(F)/\operatorname{ran}P$; in the Hilbert structures above its cokernel is represented by the kernel of the Hilbert adjoint. Composition and formal adjoint have leading symbols $\sigma(PQ)=\sigma(P)\sigma(Q)$ and $\sigma(P^*)=\sigma(P)^*$; zero leading symbol lowers the order by one. Every $P\in\Psi^m$ extends boundedly $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$, continuously in the symbol seminorms. Negative-order operators are compact on $L^2$. For elliptic $P$, the two-sided parametrix just defined yields Fredholm realizations at every integer $s$ and distributional elliptic regularity: $Pu\in C^\infty$ implies $u\in C^\infty$.

There is a positive invertible elliptic order-one operator $\Lambda_E$ on each bundle. Here positive means formally symmetric and $\langle\Lambda_Eu,u\rangle_{L^2(E)}\ge\|u\|_{L^2(E)}^2$ for every smooth section $u$; its closed realization on $L^2(E)$ has domain $H^1(E)$, and $\Lambda_E:H^1(E)\to L^2(E)$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse. Its positive scalar leading symbol $\ell(x,\xi)$ is chosen the same for all bundles over $X$. The distributional extensions $\Lambda_E:H^r(E)\to H^{r-1}(E)$ are isomorphisms for every integer $r$; $\Lambda_E^s:H^s(E)\to L^2(E)$ denotes the $s$-fold iterate when $s>0$, the inverse iterate when $s<0$, and the identity when $s=0$. In these equivalent norms the operator-norm closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ acting as $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ has a continuous surjective normalized symbol map to $C(S^*X;\operatorname{Hom}(\pi^*E,\pi^*F))$, with kernel exactly the compact operators; normalization divides the homogeneous symbol by $\ell^m$. Here $S^*X=\{(x,\xi)\in T^*X:|\xi|=1\}$.

Let $\overline\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ denote the closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ in all the seminorms $\|P\|_{H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)}$, $s\in\mathbb Z$. Its leading homogeneous symbol is continuous, and invertibility gives Fredholmness at every level and smooth kernels and adjoint kernels. The kernels are independent of $s$, and smooth data in the range have smooth preimages. Smooth symbol paths admit norm-continuous quantizations; a path continuous in the classical symbol seminorms is continuous at every indicated operator norm.

If a compact Lie group $G$ acts smoothly on $X,E,F$, write $\rho_g(y):E_y\to E_{gy}$ for its bundle action and set $(U_gu)(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, with the analogous action on $F$. Invariant density and metrics can be chosen. Conjugation $P\mapsto U_gPU_g^{-1}$ is continuous in the classical symbol seminorms and in the displayed closures. Haar averaging commutes with the symbol map and preserves these classes, orders and smooth kernels. All assertions therefore apply to $G$-invariant operators, including $G=T\times O(k)$.

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $X$ a compact smooth $G$-manifold without boundary. A compact-support symbol triple on $T^*X$ consists of finite-rank continuous complex $G$-vector bundles $A,B$ and a continuous equivariant bundle map $b:A\to B$ which is an isomorphism off a compact subset. Triples are compared by equivariant bundle isomorphisms, block sum, continuous homotopies with a common compact support, and addition or removal of elementary triples whose map is everywhere invertible. These conventions concern actual bundle maps and their deformations; no previously defined equivariant $K$-group is assumed.

Write $R(G)$ for the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional continuous complex $G$-representations. For a smooth bundle map $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, degree zero means $c(x,t\xi)=c(x,\xi)$ for all $t>0$, and elliptic means that $c(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $\xi\ne0$. For any other integer order $m$, homogeneous degree $m$ means $c(x,t\xi)=t^m c(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. An order-zero realization is a classical order-zero operator, or a simultaneous-Sobolev-closure limit of such operators, whose degree-zero principal symbol is $c$. Its $L^2$ realization is a bounded map $P:L^2(X,E)\to L^2(X,F)$. For a bounded map $T:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H_1$ between Hilbert spaces, Fredholm means that $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, $\operatorname{ran}T$ is closed, and $\operatorname{coker}T:=\mathcal H_1/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite dimensional. The Hilbert adjoint $T^*$ then has kernel unitarily isomorphic to this cokernel. For an equivariant Fredholm realization define its index to be $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]\in R(G)$, using the induced finite-dimensional $G$-representations.

Every such triple has an index $a_G(A,B,b)\in R(G)$. It is realized as $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]$ by a $G$-invariant elliptic order-zero operator on smooth bundles over $X$. Its symbol is obtained by smoothing the triple, identifying its bundles with pullbacks from the zero section by radial transport, and replacing the invertible exterior symbol by a homogeneous degree-zero symbol. The index is independent of these operations, respects all the comparisons above and is additive under block sum. For a homogeneous elliptic symbol of any integer order, it equals the Fredholm index, in the same kernel-minus-adjoint-kernel convention, of every invariant classical or simultaneous-Sobolev-closure realization with that symbol.

The construction is natural under equivariant diffeomorphisms and restriction along homomorphisms between compact Lie groups. Tensoring all data by a finite-dimensional representation tensors the index by that representation. On a point it is the difference of the two fiber representations. Let $0\to C^\infty(X,E^0)\xrightarrow{d_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{d_{N-1}}C^\infty(X,E^N)\to0$ be a finite first-order differential complex, so $d_{j+1}d_j=0$, whose positive-frequency principal-symbol sequence is exact at every nonzero real cotangent vector. For a $G$-action by chain maps with section action $U_gu(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, put $H^j=\ker d_j/\operatorname{im}d_{j-1}$, with $d_{-1}=d_N=0$. Give the bundles invariant Hermitian metrics and a positive density, and let $d_{j-1}^*$ denote the formal adjoint. The harmonic subspace in degree $j$ is $\mathcal H^j=\{u\in C^\infty(X,E^j):d_ju=0,\ d_{j-1}^*u=0\}$, with the endpoint conditions interpreted using $d_{-1}=d_N=0$; a harmonic representative of a class in $H^j$ means its representative in $\mathcal H^j$. Its symbol index is $\sum_j(-1)^j[H^j]$; these cohomology representations are finite dimensional and every class has exactly one harmonic representative. This includes the de Rham complex.

Here is the controlled noncompact form. Let $U$ have an open equivariant embedding into a compact closed smooth $G$-manifold. For a compact-support triple on $T^*U$, its index can be computed after replacing it, through the same comparisons on a neighborhood of its support, by smooth base-bundle data $E,F$ and a homogeneous degree-zero symbol $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ for which $E=F=U\times V$ and $c=I_V$ outside a compact invariant subset of $U$, with $V$ a finite-dimensional representation. There is an elliptic invariant realization equal to the exterior bundle isomorphism off one compact invariant $L\subset U$, in both the source and target kernel variables; explicitly it has the form $P=\eta_2P_0\eta_1+h(1-\eta_1)$ with nested compactly supported cutoffs and exterior isomorphism $h$. Extending the bundles and this operator to any compact equivariant ambient manifold by the exterior trivializations gives the same virtual kernel representation. Thus the index is independent of that ambient embedding and satisfies excision for open equivariant inclusions whenever such compact ambients are supplied. No compactification of an arbitrary $G$-manifold is asserted.

derivations.claim: First work in product coordinates $x\in\mathbb R^u$, $y\in\mathbb R^v$, with joint covariable $\vartheta=(\xi,\eta)$. If $a(x,\xi)$ is a classical order-one matrix symbol with compact output support, the locally output-cutoff tensor lift has symbol $q(x,y,\vartheta)=\psi(y)a(x,\xi)$. It need not be a classical joint symbol. Choose smooth scalar functions $h=1$ on $[0,1]$, $h=0$ on $[4,\infty)$, and $\chi=0$ on $[0,1]$, $\chi=1$ on $[2,\infty)$. For $0<t<1/4$ and $\vartheta\ne0$, set $c_t=h(|\xi|^2/(t^2|\vartheta|^2))$, $r_t=1-\chi(t|\vartheta|)c_t$, and $q_t=q r_t$, with $r_t=1$ near zero. For fixed $t$, $q_t$ is classical of order one: at high frequency either it vanishes near $\xi=0$ or $|\xi|\ge t|\vartheta|$, where every frequency derivative satisfies the ordinary joint symbol estimate, with constants allowed to depend on $t$. Its leading symbol is $\psi a_1(x,\xi)(1-c_t)$, uniformly within $O(t)$ on the joint unit sphere of the continuous degree-one function $\psi a_1(x,\xi)$ extended by zero at $\xi=0$.

Put $e_t=q-q_t$. On its support $|\vartheta|\ge1/t$ and $|\xi|\le2t|\vartheta|$, so $\langle\xi\rangle\le\sqrt5t|\vartheta|$. Every output derivative therefore satisfies $|\partial_{x,y}^\alpha e_t|\le C_\alpha t\langle\vartheta\rangle$, with a common compact output support and constants independent of $t$. Fourier transformation in the output variables and integration by parts $N$ times with $1-\Delta_{x,y}$ give $|\widehat e_t(\zeta,\vartheta)|\le C_N t\langle\vartheta\rangle\langle\zeta\rangle^{-2N}$. Conjugating by Sobolev weights introduces $\langle\vartheta+\zeta\rangle^{s-1}\langle\vartheta\rangle^{-s}$; the triangle inequalities for bracket weights bound the resulting kernel by $C_{N,s}t\langle\zeta\rangle^{-2N+|s-1|}$. Choose $2N>u+v+|s-1|$. Both integrals of the absolute Fourier kernel are then at most $C_st$. Weighted Cauchy--Schwarz followed by Fubini proves
$$\|\operatorname{Op}(q)-\operatorname{Op}(q_t)\|_{H^s\to H^{s-1}}\le C_st.$$
This proves simultaneous convergence at every fixed integer $s$ without requiring uniform frequency-derivative estimates for $e_t$. Multiplication on the input by a fixed smooth cutoff is bounded in these spaces. Finite fiber charts therefore prove that the genuine lift acting as the identity on the entire compact fiber lies in the joint order-one closure; the fiber cutoffs used to estimate it do not alter that operator.

Lifting is also continuous when the base operator itself belongs to the stated closure. For $s\ge1$, expand the product Sobolev norm by horizontal and vertical derivatives: an output term with $k$ horizontal derivatives and $s-1-k$ vertical derivatives is bounded by the base norm $H^{k+1}\to H^k$ applied to the same vertical derivatives of the input. Summing for $0\le k\le s-1$ bounds the lifted norm $H^s\to H^{s-1}$ by finitely many base norms. For $s=0$, Fourier transformation in the passive variable gives the bound from the base norm $L^2\to H^{-1}$, since the joint negative weight is at most the horizontal negative weight. Negative integer levels follow by duality from the corresponding positive-level bounds for the formal adjoint; the base adjoint norm $H^r\to H^{r-1}$ is exactly the original norm $H^{1-r}\to H^{-r}$. Fixed chart cutoffs contribute finitely many lower derivative terms of the same type. Approximate a closure operator by classical operators in all these base norms, lift them, and then use step 2.1 and a diagonal sequence. This gives the asserted closure lift and its continuous leading symbol. Interchanging the two factors proves the same assertion for vertical lifts.

Choose finitely many bundle charts $U_\alpha$ for $P$ and $E^i$, and smooth real functions $\phi_\alpha$ compactly supported in these charts with $\sum_\alpha\phi_\alpha^2=1$. In each chart lift the base operator $\phi_\alpha A\phi_\alpha$ to $U_\alpha\times F$ by acting in the base variable and as the identity on $G^j$. Extend by zero in the base and sum. This defines simultaneously $\widetilde A_0$ and $\widetilde A_1$, in the closure by steps 2.1–3.1. The fiber operator $B_i$ is globally defined because $B$ commutes with $H$; in every such product chart it is the fixed operator $B$ on $F$. Hence every summand commutes with both $B$ and $B^*$, with the indicated bundle types. Base cutoff multiplication also commutes with them. Choose the total density and tensor metrics as in the Statement. These patch because $H$ preserves the fiber density and metrics; the base-dependent coordinate change in $H$ has block triangular derivative, so introduces no extra density factor. Consequently the formal adjoints of the local lifts are exactly the lifts of their base formal adjoints. This proves all four stated identities before averaging.

Average both horizontal lifts over $T$ using its normalized Haar measure and their conjugation actions on the appropriate bundles. The orbit is continuous in each Sobolev norm: for a classical approximant this follows from smooth parameter-dependent chart amplitudes in [F1], and uniform boundedness of the smooth compact group action on each $H^s$ passes continuity to the closure limit. Thus the same integral exists compatibly at all integer levels. Since $B_i$ and $B_i^*$ are $T$-invariant, every conjugate still obeys the four identities; integrate them on smooth sections, where all compositions converge in every lower Sobolev norm. Invariance of the inner products makes averaging commute with formal adjoints. The resulting $A_0,A_1$ are $T$-equivariant and obey the exact displayed commutations on smooth sections. These are identities of actual operators, not merely their principal symbols.

The leading symbols of $A_0$ and $A_1$ have the form $Q(y,\zeta)\otimes I_{G^j}$ for the same continuous degree-one map $Q:p_Y^*E^0\to p_Y^*E^1$. Indeed the base local symbols act on $E$ alone; changes of associated trivialization conjugate the fiber identity to itself. On the annihilator of the vertical tangent bundle, all local base covariables identify with the covariable on $X$, so $Q(y,p_Y^*\xi)=a(p_Yy,\xi)$. Averaging preserves this equality because $a$ is equivariant. At general covectors the base-dependent $H$ transition may shift a local horizontal covariable by a term linear in the vertical covariable. It is unnecessary to assert that these local symbols coincide with a preselected connection lift. The vertical leading symbol is precisely $I_E\otimes b(y,\eta)$, where $\eta$ is restriction to the vertical tangent space; this is globally defined by $H$-equivariance.

Apply [F1] to $B$ and $B^*$ on compact $F$. Their kernels $K,L$ are finite-dimensional smooth invariant spaces. The induced $H\times T$ actions on them are smooth and unitary: the action on a fixed smooth kernel basis is smooth in every section seminorm, and its matrix entries are its $L^2$ pairings with that basis. Fiberwise $\ker B_i$ consists exactly of smooth sections of $E^i\otimes K_P$, and fiberwise $\ker B_i^*$ of sections of $E^i\otimes L_P$. This follows in each product chart by expanding a vertical kernel section in an orthonormal basis of $K$ or $L$; its coefficients are fiber integrals against that basis and are smooth in the base. The transition maps are precisely the finite-dimensional $H$ representations, so these descriptions patch to the displayed associated bundles. The orthogonal vertical kernel projections are the finite sums of these smooth rank-one kernels. They commute with the horizontal lifts and their adjoints locally, and commute with $H$ and $T$, so the same is true after gluing and averaging.

Choose a $T$-invariant principal connection, by patching local connections with a base partition and averaging their affine space over $T$. It supplies a horizontal covariable $\xi_H$ and the symbol $a_H=a(p_Yy,\xi_H)$. Interpolate $Q_r=(1-r)Q+r a_H$, $0\le r\le1$, and form the block symbol $d_r$ with $Q_r$ in place of $Q$ and $b$ in the vertical entries. Both act on different tensor factors, so
$$d_r^*d_r=\operatorname{diag}(Q_r^*Q_r\otimes I+I\otimes b^*b,\ Q_rQ_r^*\otimes I+I\otimes bb^*).$$
If $\eta\ne0$, vertical ellipticity makes both diagonal blocks positive definite. If $\eta=0$ and the joint covector is nonzero, $Q_r=a(\xi_H)$ is invertible, so they are again positive definite. The analogous $d_rd_r^*$ has the same positive summands with the $E$ parities reversed, so is positive definite by the same two cases. Compactness of the joint unit cosphere and of $[0,1]$ gives one positive lower bound on the smallest eigenvalues of both squares. Thus every $d_r$ is invertible, and $d_0$ is the actual principal symbol of $D$, while $d_1=d_{\mathrm{prod}}$. The same interpolation between two connections proves connection independence. This verifies ellipticity for arbitrary matrix symbols, with no scalar Laplacian or Dirac restriction.

Steps 3.1 and 5.1 put $D$ and its formal adjoint in the all-integer order-one closure. The continuous invertibility just proved is exactly the closure-ellipticity hypothesis of [F1], not an application of a classical parametrix to a nonsmooth joint symbol. Order reduction identifies its principal symbol with the invertible continuous degree-zero map $d_0/\ell_Y$, where $\ell_Y>0$ is the common scalar leading symbol of the order-reduction operator; the compact-kernel exact sequence supplies a parametrix modulo compact operators at every Sobolev level. In particular the range is closed and both defects are finite. A bounded parametrix gives $\|u\|_{H^s}\le C\|Du\|_{H^{s-1}}+\|Ru\|_{H^s}$ with compact $R$ on $H^s$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, compactness gives $\|Ru\|_{H^s}\le\varepsilon\|u\|_{H^s}+C_\varepsilon\|u\|_{H^{s-1}}$: otherwise a normalized violating sequence has weaker norm tending to zero, hence is weakly zero in $H^s$ by smooth dual-test density, contradicting compactness of $R$. Absorb $\varepsilon<1$ to obtain
$$\|u\|_{H^s}\le C_s\bigl(\|Du\|_{H^{s-1}}+\|u\|_{H^{s-1}}\bigr)$$
with the analogous estimate for the adjoint. Smoothness of the defects is also covered by [F1]; equivalently, approximate in any two chosen Sobolev norms by one sufficiently close classical elliptic representative. Fredholm openness gives the same index at these levels, because its classical symbol is uniformly close to $d_0$. The kernels decrease as the Sobolev level increases and the adjoint kernels representing cokernels increase at the dual level. Equality of the two indices forces both dimensions to be unchanged. Repeating over all integers identifies each defect with its smooth intersection. Thus the energy calculations below apply to every kernel vector of the $H^1\to L^2$ realization.

For smooth inputs, expand the squared norm using the product inner products. The cross terms are $-2\operatorname{Re}\langle B_1A_0u,v\rangle+2\operatorname{Re}\langle A_1B_0u,v\rangle$ and cancel by step 5.1. Therefore
$$\|D(u,v)\|^2=\|A_0u\|^2+\|B_0u\|^2+\|A_1^*v\|^2+\|B_1^*v\|^2.$$
For $D^*(w,z)=(A_0^*w+B_0^*z,-B_1w+A_1z)$ the cross terms cancel using $B_0A_0^*=A_1^*B_1$, giving
$$\|D^*(w,z)\|^2=\|A_0^*w\|^2+\|B_1w\|^2+\|A_1z\|^2+\|B_0^*z\|^2.$$
It follows, now for the actual Fredholm kernels by step 8.1, that $\ker D=(\ker A_0\cap\ker B_0)\oplus(\ker A_1^*\cap\ker B_1^*)$ and $\ker D^*=(\ker A_0^*\cap\ker B_1)\oplus(\ker A_1\cap\ker B_0^*)$. No cancellation of unbounded operator products on unspecified domains is used: the identities were first proved on smooth sections, and all kernel vectors are smooth.

Restrict $A_0$ to the $K$-kernel bundle and $A_1$ to the $L$-kernel bundle. They are respectively $C_K$ and $C_L$. In local charts they are the base operators tensored with the identity of the finite-dimensional spaces $K,L$; their symbols are $a\otimes I$. Hence they are elliptic closure operators on the compact base and have smooth Fredholm defects by [F1]. Since the vertical projections are orthogonal and commute with both horizontal operators and adjoints, the restrictions of $A_0^*$ and $A_1^*$ are exactly $C_K^*$ and $C_L^*$, with no compression error. The four intersections in step 9.1 are therefore $\ker C_K$, $\ker C_L^*$, $\ker C_K^*$ and $\ker C_L$, respectively. All identifications commute with $T$. Taking their virtual representation difference gives
$$[\ker D]-[\ker D^*]=([\ker C_K]-[\ker C_K^*])-([\ker C_L]-[\ker C_L^*]),$$
the claimed associated-bundle formula.

By [F2] and the explicit elliptic homotopy in step 7.1, the index of $D$ is the analytic symbol index of the graded product. Replacing $C_K,C_L$ by any equivariant elliptic quantizations with the same twisted symbols leaves their indices unchanged. For a genuine product choose the global tensor lift instead of the patched lift. Then $C_K=A\otimes I_K$ and $C_L=A\otimes I_L$. Their kernel and adjoint-kernel spaces are the tensor products of the corresponding defects of $A$ with $K,L$; the Fredholm estimates and a finite orthonormal basis of $K,L$ prove this directly. The representation difference is $\operatorname{Ind}A\otimes(\ker B-\ker B^*)$. Applying this construction with the product of the independently acting compact groups proves the external representation-index product, and restriction proves the version for a diagonal action.

For compactly supported symbols on invariant open manifolds, choose the controlled representatives of [F2] in compactifications, stabilize them if needed, and use its order reduction to make their homogeneous order one representatives. Form the compact product just proved. For compact-support triples representing the two data sets, the tensor complex is contractible wherever either map is invertible: a contracting homotopy for that factor, tensored with the identity and the usual grading, contracts the total differential because the cross terms cancel. Its nonexactness set is therefore contained in the product of the prescribed compact supports. The homogeneous order normalization represents this same product class by [F2]. The controlled realization of that product class has kernel supported in a compact subset of the product open set in both variables. Excision identifies its index with that in the compact product, whose symbol index is already the product of the two indices by step 11.1. A different compactification gives the same result by the two-variable kernel/adjoint-kernel restriction argument of [F2]. Empty manifolds, zero-rank coefficient bundles and zero-dimensional fibers give the same identities with zero operators or finite matrices. In dimension zero the closure estimate is just a finite-dimensional norm estimate. All compact-group averages and Hilbert constructions retain the stated AC hypothesis.
