Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, put $n=\dim X$, and fix a smooth Riemannian metric, a positive density, and Hermitian metrics on smooth finite-rank complex bundles $E,F\to X$. Let $\pi:T^*X\to X$ be the bundle projection, use the dual metric to define $|\xi|$ and $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$, and use the induced operator norm for local symbol matrices. In a coordinate chart and local bundle frames, a symbol of integer order $m$ is a smooth matrix $p(x,\xi)$ satisfying, on each compact coordinate subset,

$$|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\langle\xi\rangle^{m-|\beta|}.$$

A classical symbol also has homogeneous terms $p_{m-j}(x,\xi)$, smooth for $\xi\ne0$, such that subtracting the first $N$ terms, multiplied by a cutoff zero near $\xi=0$ and one for large $\xi$, gives a symbol of order $m-N$. Quantization means

$$\operatorname{Op}(p)u(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}p(x,\xi)\widehat u(\xi)\,d\xi,\qquad\widehat u(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx,$$

localized by smooth cutoffs in source and target. Define $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ to be operators given by finite sums of these local classical quantizations and operators with smooth kernels. Define integer Sobolev spaces by finite-chart Fourier norms $\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat u\|_2$, using distributions for negative $s$; different finite-chart choices give equivalent norms.

This class is independent of charts and frames. Its leading symbol is a well-defined smooth homogeneous bundle map $\sigma_m(P):\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, satisfying $\sigma_m(P)(x,t\xi)=t^m\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. Every such map is realized. Call $P$ elliptic when $\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $(x,\xi)$ with $\xi\ne0$. A two-sided parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ is an operator $Q\in\Psi^{-m}(X;F,E)$ such that $QP-I_E$ and $PQ-I_F$ are operators with smooth Schwartz kernels. A Fredholm realization at Sobolev level $s$ is the bounded map $P:H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range, and finite-dimensional cokernel $H^{s-m}(F)/\operatorname{ran}P$; in the Hilbert structures above its cokernel is represented by the kernel of the Hilbert adjoint. Composition and formal adjoint have leading symbols $\sigma(PQ)=\sigma(P)\sigma(Q)$ and $\sigma(P^*)=\sigma(P)^*$; zero leading symbol lowers the order by one. Every $P\in\Psi^m$ extends boundedly $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$, continuously in the symbol seminorms. Negative-order operators are compact on $L^2$. For elliptic $P$, the two-sided parametrix just defined yields Fredholm realizations at every integer $s$ and distributional elliptic regularity: $Pu\in C^\infty$ implies $u\in C^\infty$.

There is a positive invertible elliptic order-one operator $\Lambda_E$ on each bundle. Here positive means formally symmetric and $\langle\Lambda_Eu,u\rangle_{L^2(E)}\ge\|u\|_{L^2(E)}^2$ for every smooth section $u$; its closed realization on $L^2(E)$ has domain $H^1(E)$, and $\Lambda_E:H^1(E)\to L^2(E)$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse. Its positive scalar leading symbol $\ell(x,\xi)$ is chosen the same for all bundles over $X$. The distributional extensions $\Lambda_E:H^r(E)\to H^{r-1}(E)$ are isomorphisms for every integer $r$; $\Lambda_E^s:H^s(E)\to L^2(E)$ denotes the $s$-fold iterate when $s>0$, the inverse iterate when $s<0$, and the identity when $s=0$. In these equivalent norms the operator-norm closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ acting as $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ has a continuous surjective normalized symbol map to $C(S^*X;\operatorname{Hom}(\pi^*E,\pi^*F))$, with kernel exactly the compact operators; normalization divides the homogeneous symbol by $\ell^m$. Here $S^*X=\{(x,\xi)\in T^*X:|\xi|=1\}$.

Let $\overline\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ denote the closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ in all the seminorms $\|P\|_{H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)}$, $s\in\mathbb Z$. Its leading homogeneous symbol is continuous, and invertibility gives Fredholmness at every level and smooth kernels and adjoint kernels. The kernels are independent of $s$, and smooth data in the range have smooth preimages. Smooth symbol paths admit norm-continuous quantizations; a path continuous in the classical symbol seminorms is continuous at every indicated operator norm.

If a compact Lie group $G$ acts smoothly on $X,E,F$, write $\rho_g(y):E_y\to E_{gy}$ for its bundle action and set $(U_gu)(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, with the analogous action on $F$. Invariant density and metrics can be chosen. Conjugation $P\mapsto U_gPU_g^{-1}$ is continuous in the classical symbol seminorms and in the displayed closures. Haar averaging commutes with the symbol map and preserves these classes, orders and smooth kernels. All assertions therefore apply to $G$-invariant operators, including $G=T\times O(k)$.

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $X$ a compact smooth $G$-manifold without boundary. A compact-support symbol triple on $T^*X$ consists of finite-rank continuous complex $G$-vector bundles $A,B$ and a continuous equivariant bundle map $b:A\to B$ which is an isomorphism off a compact subset. Triples are compared by equivariant bundle isomorphisms, block sum, continuous homotopies with a common compact support, and addition or removal of elementary triples whose map is everywhere invertible. These conventions concern actual bundle maps and their deformations; no previously defined equivariant $K$-group is assumed.

Write $R(G)$ for the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional continuous complex $G$-representations. For a smooth bundle map $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, degree zero means $c(x,t\xi)=c(x,\xi)$ for all $t>0$, and elliptic means that $c(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $\xi\ne0$. For any other integer order $m$, homogeneous degree $m$ means $c(x,t\xi)=t^m c(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. An order-zero realization is a classical order-zero operator, or a simultaneous-Sobolev-closure limit of such operators, whose degree-zero principal symbol is $c$. Its $L^2$ realization is a bounded map $P:L^2(X,E)\to L^2(X,F)$. For a bounded map $T:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H_1$ between Hilbert spaces, Fredholm means that $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, $\operatorname{ran}T$ is closed, and $\operatorname{coker}T:=\mathcal H_1/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite dimensional. The Hilbert adjoint $T^*$ then has kernel unitarily isomorphic to this cokernel. For an equivariant Fredholm realization define its index to be $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]\in R(G)$, using the induced finite-dimensional $G$-representations.

Every such triple has an index $a_G(A,B,b)\in R(G)$. It is realized as $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]$ by a $G$-invariant elliptic order-zero operator on smooth bundles over $X$. Its symbol is obtained by smoothing the triple, identifying its bundles with pullbacks from the zero section by radial transport, and replacing the invertible exterior symbol by a homogeneous degree-zero symbol. The index is independent of these operations, respects all the comparisons above and is additive under block sum. For a homogeneous elliptic symbol of any integer order, it equals the Fredholm index, in the same kernel-minus-adjoint-kernel convention, of every invariant classical or simultaneous-Sobolev-closure realization with that symbol.

The construction is natural under equivariant diffeomorphisms and restriction along homomorphisms between compact Lie groups. Tensoring all data by a finite-dimensional representation tensors the index by that representation. On a point it is the difference of the two fiber representations. Let $0\to C^\infty(X,E^0)\xrightarrow{d_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{d_{N-1}}C^\infty(X,E^N)\to0$ be a finite first-order differential complex, so $d_{j+1}d_j=0$, whose positive-frequency principal-symbol sequence is exact at every nonzero real cotangent vector. For a $G$-action by chain maps with section action $U_gu(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, put $H^j=\ker d_j/\operatorname{im}d_{j-1}$, with $d_{-1}=d_N=0$. Give the bundles invariant Hermitian metrics and a positive density, and let $d_{j-1}^*$ denote the formal adjoint. The harmonic subspace in degree $j$ is $\mathcal H^j=\{u\in C^\infty(X,E^j):d_ju=0,\ d_{j-1}^*u=0\}$, with the endpoint conditions interpreted using $d_{-1}=d_N=0$; a harmonic representative of a class in $H^j$ means its representative in $\mathcal H^j$. Its symbol index is $\sum_j(-1)^j[H^j]$; these cohomology representations are finite dimensional and every class has exactly one harmonic representative. This includes the de Rham complex.

Here is the controlled noncompact form. Let $U$ have an open equivariant embedding into a compact closed smooth $G$-manifold. For a compact-support triple on $T^*U$, its index can be computed after replacing it, through the same comparisons on a neighborhood of its support, by smooth base-bundle data $E,F$ and a homogeneous degree-zero symbol $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ for which $E=F=U\times V$ and $c=I_V$ outside a compact invariant subset of $U$, with $V$ a finite-dimensional representation. There is an elliptic invariant realization equal to the exterior bundle isomorphism off one compact invariant $L\subset U$, in both the source and target kernel variables; explicitly it has the form $P=\eta_2P_0\eta_1+h(1-\eta_1)$ with nested compactly supported cutoffs and exterior isomorphism $h$. Extending the bundles and this operator to any compact equivariant ambient manifold by the exterior trivializations gives the same virtual kernel representation. Thus the index is independent of that ambient embedding and satisfies excision for open equivariant inclusions whenever such compact ambients are supplied. No compactification of an arbitrary $G$-manifold is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $T$ and $H$ be compact Lie groups, with no connectedness or commutativity requirement on $H$. For any compact Lie group $K$, write $R(K)$ for the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional continuous complex $K$-representations. Let $P\to X$ be a smooth principal right $H$-bundle over a compact smooth manifold without boundary. Let $T$ act smoothly on $P$ on the left, commuting with $H$, and let $F$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary with commuting smooth left actions of $H$ and $T$. Put $Y=P\times_H F$, where $(p h,f)$ is identified with $(p,hf)$, and let $p_Y:Y\to X$ be its projection. The action of $t\in T$ on $Y$ is $[p,f]\mapsto[tp,tf]$.

Let $E^0,E^1\to X$ be smooth Hermitian $T$-bundles and $G^0,G^1\to F$ smooth Hermitian $H\times T$-bundles. Choose invariant densities and metrics. Let $A:C^\infty(X,E^0)\to C^\infty(X,E^1)$ and $B:C^\infty(F,G^0)\to C^\infty(F,G^1)$ be respectively $T$- and $H\times T$-equivariant operators of order one, either classical or in the order-one Sobolev closure. In the latter case, classical order-one operators converge to the given operator in every norm $H^s\to H^{s-1}$, $s\in\mathbb Z$, and their compatible degree-one principal symbols converge to its continuous degree-one principal symbol. Degree one means $a(x,t\xi)=t a(x,\xi)$ and $b(f,t\eta)=t b(f,\eta)$ for $t>0$; the symbols are smooth in the classical case and continuous in the closure case. Elliptic means that the corresponding symbol is a linear isomorphism at every nonzero covector. Extend $a(x,\xi)$ and $b(f,\eta)$ by zero at the zero covector, and assume $A$ and $B$ are elliptic.

Write $\mathcal G^j=P\times_H G^j\to Y$ and $\mathcal E^{ij}=p_Y^*E^i\otimes\mathcal G^j$. The horizontal lifts below are defined by this finite-chart construction. Choose a finite cover $\{U_\alpha\}$ of $X$ trivializing $P$ and the bundles $E^0,E^1$, and smooth real functions $\phi_\alpha$ compactly supported in $U_\alpha$ with $\sum_\alpha\phi_\alpha^2=1$. In the induced product chart $Y|_{U_\alpha}\cong U_\alpha\times F$, lift $\phi_\alpha A\phi_\alpha$ by acting in the base variable on the $E^i$ factor and by the identity on $G^j$; extend this operator by zero outside the chart and sum the finite family to obtain $\widetilde A_j$. Let $\rho_t^{ij}(y):\mathcal E^{ij}_y\to\mathcal E^{ij}_{ty}$ be the induced bundle action and define the section action by $U_t^{ij}s(y)=\rho_t^{ij}(t^{-1}y)s(t^{-1}y)$. Set

$$A_j=\int_T U_t^{1j}\widetilde A_j(U_t^{0j})^{-1}\,dt,$$

where $dt$ is normalized Haar probability and the integral is taken in each $H^s(Y,\mathcal E^{0j})\to H^{s-1}(Y,\mathcal E^{1j})$ operator norm. The resulting operator acts on smooth sections and is a common order-one Sobolev-closure limit, bounded in every such norm for $s\in\mathbb Z$. The connection used in the product-symbol formula below splits covectors on $Y$; the lifts are the chartwise operators just defined.

Thus the domains and codomains of the compatible $T$-equivariant lifts are

$$A_j:C^\infty(Y,\mathcal E^{0j})\longrightarrow C^\infty(Y,\mathcal E^{1j}),\qquad j=0,1.$$

Let $B_i:C^\infty(Y,\mathcal E^{i0})\to C^\infty(Y,\mathcal E^{i1})$ denote the operator whose restriction over each base point $x\in X$ is $B$ acting on the $F$-fiber, tensored with the fixed vector space $E_x^i$. On smooth sections these lifts obey all four exact identities

$$B_1A_0=A_1B_0,\qquad B_0^*A_1^*=A_0^*B_1^*,\qquad B_1^*A_1=A_0B_0^*,\qquad B_0A_0^*=A_1^*B_1.$$

The adjoints are with respect to the invariant product density on $Y$ obtained from the base density and the $H$-invariant fiber density. Define

$$D=\begin{pmatrix}A_0&-B_1^*\\ B_0&A_1^*\end{pmatrix}:\mathcal E^{00}\oplus\mathcal E^{11}\longrightarrow\mathcal E^{10}\oplus\mathcal E^{01}.$$

In this calculus, an order-one operator on $Y$ is elliptic when its continuous joint degree-one principal symbol is a bundle isomorphism at every nonzero covector of $T^*Y$. The operator $D$ extends boundedly from $H^1(Y,\mathcal E^{00}\oplus\mathcal E^{11})$ to $L^2(Y,\mathcal E^{10}\oplus\mathcal E^{01})$. Fredholm means that this bounded map has finite-dimensional kernel, closed range, and finite-dimensional cokernel, the quotient of the target by its range; its Hilbert adjoint is taken in the stated $L^2$ structures.

Then $D:H^1\to L^2$ is Fredholm, both its kernel and its adjoint kernel are finite-dimensional smooth $T$-representations, and its principal symbol represents the graded product of $a$ and $b$. Explicitly, a connection splitting of a covector on $Y$ into horizontal $\xi$ and vertical $\eta$ gives the product symbol

$$d_{\mathrm{prod}}(y;\xi,\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}a(p_Yy,\xi)\otimes I&-I\otimes b(f,\eta)^*\\ I\otimes b(f,\eta)&a(p_Yy,\xi)^*\otimes I\end{pmatrix}.$$

This matrix is interpreted using an associated-bundle trivialization; its homotopy class is independent of the connection. The actual glued lift symbol need only be homotopic through invertible joint symbols to this matrix.

Let $K=\ker B$ and $L=\ker B^*$, with their finite-dimensional $H\times T$ actions, and put $K_P=P\times_H K$, $L_P=P\times_H L$. The restricted lifts give elliptic operators $C_K:E^0\otimes K_P\to E^1\otimes K_P$ and $C_L$ with $K$ replaced by $L$, whose symbols are $a\otimes I$. For $\operatorname{Ind}_T Q=[\ker Q]-[\ker Q^*]\in R(T)$ one has

$$\operatorname{Ind}_T D=\operatorname{Ind}_T C_K-\operatorname{Ind}_T C_L.$$

Thus the analytic symbol index of the associated product is the base symbol index twisted by the associated virtual vertical index $K_P-L_P$. For a product bundle with independent commuting group actions this specializes to multiplication of representation-valued indices. The same external-product identity holds for compactly supported elliptic symbol data on invariant open manifolds when their indices are defined by the controlled compactification and excision construction.
For $n\ge1$, $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^n)$ is $\mathbb R$ in degrees $0,n$ and zero otherwise. For $S^0$ it is $\mathbb R^2$ in degree zero and zero otherwise.

With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation, $$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$ An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point

Then $$K^0(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z[\beta]/(\beta^2),\qquad \widetilde K^0(S^2)=\mathbb Z\beta.$$ Restriction to a point is projection onto the integer summand. The sign of $\beta$ is tied to the stated clutching convention.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], use the controlled symbol classes and realizations from [F2] throughout. Exterior multiplication satisfies $\varepsilon_z^2=0$ and $\varepsilon_z\varepsilon_z^*+\varepsilon_z^*\varepsilon_z=|z|^2I$: verify first for an orthonormal basis and use bilinearity. Hence the stated square identity and compact-support class hold. Under $V=V_1\oplus V_2$, the exterior-algebra identification gives $k_{V}(z_1,z_2)=k_{V_1}(z_1)\widehat\otimes1+1\widehat\otimes k_{V_2}(z_2)$. This is exactly the graded symbol product, with no extra sign. Thus $b_{V_1\oplus V_2}=b_{V_1}\boxtimes b_{V_2}$, equivariantly for any group preserving the decomposition. For a real orthogonal bundle the real metric extends complex-bilinearly to identify its complexification with its complex dual. The same doubled-real Bott convention can therefore be written with the dual, while such an identification is not asserted for arbitrary complex bundles.

We first fix the nonequivariant line sign explicitly. On $S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ let $P_+$ project onto $e^{inx}$, $n\ge0$, and put $A=e^{ix}P_++1-P_+$. The Fejér kernels show that trigonometric polynomials are dense in $L^2$: they approximate continuous functions uniformly, and continuous functions approximate interval indicators and hence simple functions in $L^2$. Thus the Fourier vectors are a complete orthonormal basis. The map $A$ sends the $n$th vector to the $(n+1)$st for $n\ge0$ and to itself for $n<0$. Its images are exactly all nonzero modes, orthonormally, so $\ker A=0$, its range is closed and its cokernel is the constants. Its index is $-1$. To check its actual symbol, localize with a smooth function $f$ in an interval of length less than $2\pi$. The local symbol of $P_+$ is $(2\pi)^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}\widehat f(n-\xi)e^{ix(n-\xi)}$. For $\xi\to-\infty$ this and every derivative decrease faster than every power, by rapid decay of the Fourier transform of $f$. For $\xi\to+\infty$ subtract the rapidly decreasing sum over $n<0$ from the full Fourier reconstruction $f(x)$. The resulting estimates, also off the diagonal, prove that $P_+$ is classical of order zero with leading symbol $1$ on $\xi>0$ and $0$ on $\xi<0$. Thus $A$ has symbol $e^{ix}$ on the positive ray and $1$ on the negative ray.

The compact de Rham operator has index its cohomological Euler representation, as follows directly from [F1]. On a compact invariant Riemannian manifold let $D=d+d^*$, acting from even to odd complex forms, with the usual group action on forms. Integration by parts gives $D^2=\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$ and $\langle\Delta u,u\rangle=\|du\|^2+\|d^*u\|^2$. The principal symbol of $D$ is $i(\varepsilon_\xi-\varepsilon_\xi^*)$, so it is elliptic. The parametrix and regularity give smooth finite-dimensional kernels and closed range; since the self-adjoint elliptic $\Delta$ has cokernel its kernel, its restriction to the orthogonal complement of its kernel is invertible, with inverse $G$ improving Sobolev order by two. For closed smooth $\alpha$ write $\alpha=h+\Delta G\alpha$. Commutation $d\Delta=\Delta d$ shows $dG\alpha$ is harmonic; it is exact, so its norm vanishes by integration by parts against its primitive. Hence $\alpha=h+dd^*G\alpha$. A harmonic exact form is zero by the same norm calculation. Thus harmonic forms identify with cohomology, equivariantly because all operations commute with the compact action. This proves the stated index comparison here without invoking a scalar Hodge assertion for a matrix complex.

Homotope the loop $e^{ix}$ to $e^{i\varphi(x)}$, where $\varphi$ rises smoothly from $0$ to $2\pi$ inside a proper coordinate interval and is constant near the ends; the homotopy is $e^{i((1-t)x+t\varphi(x))}$. It is smooth periodic, including at the cut, and preserves symbol invertibility on both rays. The final symbol is extended from the interval. On its cotangent plane a representative is $1+(e^{i\varphi(x)}-1)h(\xi)$, where $h=0$ for $\xi\le-1$ and $h=1$ for $\xi\ge1$. Its only possible zeros lie in a compact rectangle. On the rectangle it is $e^{i\varphi(x)}$ on the top and $1$ elsewhere. With orientation $dx\wedge d\xi$, the top is traversed right to left, so its winding is $-1$. More explicitly its boundary loop divided by $\bar z$ on a disk has winding zero and a continuous logarithm, so a logarithm homotopy identifies it with $\bar z$. The loops $z\oplus\bar z$ contract to a constant invertible matrix through $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t z&-\sqrt{1-t^2}\\\sqrt{1-t^2}&t\bar z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ for $1\ge t\ge0$. Consequently this relative class is $-b_{\mathbb R}$. By symbol homotopy, excision and step 1.2, $a_{\{1\}}(b_{\mathbb R})=1$. This establishes the sign independently of de Rham dimensions.

We next prove a symbol identity on $S^m\subset\mathbb R^m\oplus\mathbb R$, for $m=1,2$, equivariantly under $O(m)$ acting on the first summand. The de Rham symbol is equivalent to the Koszul symbol of the real covector $\xi$: on exterior degree $k$, multiplication by $i^k$ conjugates $\varepsilon_\xi+\varepsilon_\xi^*$ to $i(\varepsilon_\xi-\varepsilon_\xi^*)$. Use the round metric to identify exterior covectors and vectors. Let $f(q,t)=t$ be the smooth invariant height function and deform this real Koszul symbol to exterior multiplication by $\xi+is\,df$, plus its adjoint, for $0\le s\le1$. This is a globally smooth equivariant symbol on the same bundles. Real and imaginary parts are orthogonal in the Hermitian norm, so its square is $(|\xi|^2+s^2|df|^2)I$. At $s=0$ its noninvertibility is the zero section; for $s>0$ it is precisely the zero covectors over the two critical points of $f$, the north and south poles. Thus the full homotopy has one common compact noninvertibility set, the zero section. No comparison of only the principal symbols is being substituted for this compact-support homotopy.

The two pole classes have the following exact signs. In the north and south stereographic disk coordinates $x\mapsto(2x/(1+|x|^2),\pm(1-|x|^2)/(1+|x|^2))$, the round metric is $c(x)^2\sum_jdx_j^2$ with $c(x)=2/(1+|x|^2)$, and $df=\mp4\sum_jx_jdx_j/(1+|x|^2)^2$. If $\eta$ is the canonical cotangent coordinate, the orthonormal coframe coefficients of $\xi+i\,df$ are $c^{-1}(\eta\mp i a(x)x)$, where $a(x)=4/(1+|x|^2)^2>0$. The real orthonormal frames identify the exterior bundles equivariantly with $\Lambda^\bullet\mathbb C^m$. Positive scalar multiplication by $c$ preserves their class. Excision into disjoint pole neighborhoods is permitted because the final symbol is invertible on their complement; adding elementary symbols and gluing along that invertible map is precisely open extension for compact-support triples. On each neighborhood the homotopy $a_t=(1-t)a+t>0$ changes the symbol to $\eta\mp ix$, keeping its sole zero at $(0,0)$. On the north, multiplication of its vector by $i$ gives $x+i\eta$. On the south it gives $-x+i\eta$, and subsequent multiplication by $-1$ gives $x-i\eta$. Scalar unit complex multiplications are joined to the identity through unit scalars, preserve equivariance and introduce no zeros. With $\vartheta(x,\eta)=(x,-\eta)$ and open extensions $j_0,j_\infty$ from the pole charts, the actual symbol identity is $[\sigma(D_{S^m})]=j_0b_{\mathbb R^m}+j_\infty\vartheta^*b_{\mathbb R^m}$. This proves both the compact support and the two local signs without a continuous-to-smooth sphere gluing premise.

The sphere map interchanging the two hemispheres is $O(m)$-equivariant and carries their chosen tangent coordinates into one another. Excision and diffeomorphism covariance therefore give $a_{O(m)}(\sigma(D_{S^m}))=a_{O(m)}(b_{\mathbb R^m})+a_{O(m)}(\vartheta^*b_{\mathbb R^m})$. For $m=1$ let $\epsilon$ be the nontrivial character of $O(1)$. The class identity $\vartheta^*b_{\mathbb R}=-\epsilon b_{\mathbb R}$ is explicit. On the unit complex circle the direct sum on the left of $\vartheta^*b+\epsilon b=0$ has domain $1\oplus\epsilon$ and, after exchanging target summands, matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&z\\\bar z&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The path $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\sin t&\cos t\,z\\\cos t\,\bar z&-\sin t\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $0\le t\le\pi/2$, is equivariant for the involution $z\mapsto-z$ and the matrix representation $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, is invertible since its determinant is $-1$, and ends at a constant equivariant isomorphism. Hence the sum is zero as a relative class. For $m=2$ restricted to $SO(2)$, $\vartheta$ is properly equivariantly homotopic to the identity by $(x,\xi)\mapsto(x,R_{\pi t}\xi)$; on the symbols its square norm remains $|x|^2+|\xi|^2$. Thus $\vartheta^*b=b$ for this group.

On the circle, constants generate $H^0$ and $dx$ generates $H^1$; reflection acts by $1$ and $-1$, respectively. Hence step 1.3 gives $a_{O(1)}(\sigma(D_{S^1}))=1-\epsilon$. If $r=a_{O(1)}(b_{\mathbb R})=u+v\epsilon$, step 4.1 gives $(1-\epsilon)r=1-\epsilon$, or $u-v=1$. Restriction to the trivial group and step 2.1 give $u+v=1$. Thus $u=1,v=0$: this is the full $O(1)$ representation, not just its dimension. On $S^2$, [F4] gives only $H^0$ and $H^2$; the invariant area form has nonzero integral and is therefore not exact, so it generates the latter group. Both representations are trivial under rotations. Thus $a_{SO(2)}(\sigma(D_{S^2}))=2$. Step 4.1 implies $2a_{SO(2)}(b_{\mathbb R^2})=2$. By [F2], averaging a positive Hermitian form makes every finite-dimensional representation unitary. To see directly that $R(SO(2))$ has no torsion, let $\rho:SO(2)\to U(W)$ be any such continuous representation and set $P_k w=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{-ikt}\rho(R_t)w\,dt$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$. Changing variables in the integral gives $\rho(R_s)P_kw=e^{iks}P_kw$, so each $P_kw$ is a weight vector or zero. For fixed $w$, the Fejér means of the continuous periodic function $t\mapsto\rho(R_t)w$ at $0$ are finite linear combinations of these $P_kw$ and converge to $w$: the Fejér kernel is nonnegative with integral one, and its mass outside every neighborhood of zero tends to zero, so uniform continuity proves uniform convergence of its convolutions. Since $W$ is finite-dimensional, the span of all weight spaces is closed and contains every $w$. Distinct weights form a direct sum, as applying the corresponding Fourier projections isolates each weight. Thus $W$ is a direct sum of characters $z\mapsto z^m$, $m\in\mathbb Z$, and virtual representations are uniquely determined by their integer multiplicities; multiplication by $2$ is injective in $R(SO(2))$. Therefore $2a_{SO(2)}(b_{\mathbb R^2})=2$ implies $a_{SO(2)}(b_{\mathbb R^2})=1$.

Every orthogonal matrix $Q$ on $V$ admits an orthogonal decomposition into invariant real lines with eigenvalue $+1$ or $-1$, and real planes on which it is a rotation: diagonalize its complex unitary complexification and pair conjugate eigenvectors; real eigenvectors span the remaining $\pm1$ spaces. Thus $Q$ belongs to a block subgroup $H$ which is a product of copies of $O(1)$ and $SO(2)$. On restriction to this entire subgroup, step 1.1 identifies $b_V$ with the product of the line and plane symbols. By [F3] and step 5.1 its index is $1\in R(H)$. Restriction of a Fredholm index simply restricts its finite kernel representations, so the character of $a_{O(n)}(b_V)$ takes the value $1$ at the original arbitrary matrix $Q$. This proves equality of characters on every component of $O(n)$, including orientation-reversing matrices.

Equality of these characters implies equality in $R(O(n))$. Indeed average inner products over $O(n)$ to make representations unitary, and take invariant orthogonal complements to decompose them into irreducibles. Normalized invariant volume on $O(n)$ can be obtained from the bi-invariant metric induced by the trace inner product on its skew-symmetric matrices, giving equal mass to its two components. Averaging on $\operatorname{Hom}(U,W)$ is the orthogonal projection onto intertwining maps, so the integral of $\overline{\chi_U}\chi_W$ is their dimension; for irreducibles this is $1$ if isomorphic and $0$ otherwise, by Schur's lemma (an eigenvalue of an intertwiner and its invariant kernel prove that lemma over $\mathbb C$). Pairing a zero virtual character against every irreducible therefore gives zero multiplicities. Apply this to step 6.1 minus the trivial character to obtain $a_{O(n)}(b_V)=1$. For $n=0$ the open Euclidean set is a point and its symbol is the even line, whose index is directly $1$. Group restriction and coefficient tensoring in [F2] give the general assertion. Finally the complex orientation is the ordered product $dx_1\wedge d\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n\wedge d\xi_n$, whereas $(d\theta)^n/n!$ is its $(-1)^n$ multiple, proving the exact orientation convention.

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, put $n=\dim X$, and fix a smooth Riemannian metric, a positive density, and Hermitian metrics on smooth finite-rank complex bundles $E,F\to X$. Let $\pi:T^*X\to X$ be the bundle projection, use the dual metric to define $|\xi|$ and $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$, and use the induced operator norm for local symbol matrices. In a coordinate chart and local bundle frames, a symbol of integer order $m$ is a smooth matrix $p(x,\xi)$ satisfying, on each compact coordinate subset,

$$|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\langle\xi\rangle^{m-|\beta|}.$$

A classical symbol also has homogeneous terms $p_{m-j}(x,\xi)$, smooth for $\xi\ne0$, such that subtracting the first $N$ terms, multiplied by a cutoff zero near $\xi=0$ and one for large $\xi$, gives a symbol of order $m-N$. Quantization means

$$\operatorname{Op}(p)u(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}p(x,\xi)\widehat u(\xi)\,d\xi,\qquad\widehat u(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx,$$

localized by smooth cutoffs in source and target. Define $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ to be operators given by finite sums of these local classical quantizations and operators with smooth kernels. Define integer Sobolev spaces by finite-chart Fourier norms $\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat u\|_2$, using distributions for negative $s$; different finite-chart choices give equivalent norms.

This class is independent of charts and frames. Its leading symbol is a well-defined smooth homogeneous bundle map $\sigma_m(P):\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, satisfying $\sigma_m(P)(x,t\xi)=t^m\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. Every such map is realized. Call $P$ elliptic when $\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $(x,\xi)$ with $\xi\ne0$. A two-sided parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ is an operator $Q\in\Psi^{-m}(X;F,E)$ such that $QP-I_E$ and $PQ-I_F$ are operators with smooth Schwartz kernels. A Fredholm realization at Sobolev level $s$ is the bounded map $P:H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range, and finite-dimensional cokernel $H^{s-m}(F)/\operatorname{ran}P$; in the Hilbert structures above its cokernel is represented by the kernel of the Hilbert adjoint. Composition and formal adjoint have leading symbols $\sigma(PQ)=\sigma(P)\sigma(Q)$ and $\sigma(P^*)=\sigma(P)^*$; zero leading symbol lowers the order by one. Every $P\in\Psi^m$ extends boundedly $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$, continuously in the symbol seminorms. Negative-order operators are compact on $L^2$. For elliptic $P$, the two-sided parametrix just defined yields Fredholm realizations at every integer $s$ and distributional elliptic regularity: $Pu\in C^\infty$ implies $u\in C^\infty$.

There is a positive invertible elliptic order-one operator $\Lambda_E$ on each bundle. Here positive means formally symmetric and $\langle\Lambda_Eu,u\rangle_{L^2(E)}\ge\|u\|_{L^2(E)}^2$ for every smooth section $u$; its closed realization on $L^2(E)$ has domain $H^1(E)$, and $\Lambda_E:H^1(E)\to L^2(E)$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse. Its positive scalar leading symbol $\ell(x,\xi)$ is chosen the same for all bundles over $X$. The distributional extensions $\Lambda_E:H^r(E)\to H^{r-1}(E)$ are isomorphisms for every integer $r$; $\Lambda_E^s:H^s(E)\to L^2(E)$ denotes the $s$-fold iterate when $s>0$, the inverse iterate when $s<0$, and the identity when $s=0$. In these equivalent norms the operator-norm closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ acting as $H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)$ has a continuous surjective normalized symbol map to $C(S^*X;\operatorname{Hom}(\pi^*E,\pi^*F))$, with kernel exactly the compact operators; normalization divides the homogeneous symbol by $\ell^m$. Here $S^*X=\{(x,\xi)\in T^*X:|\xi|=1\}$.

Let $\overline\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ denote the closure of $\Psi^m(X;E,F)$ in all the seminorms $\|P\|_{H^s(E)\to H^{s-m}(F)}$, $s\in\mathbb Z$. Its leading homogeneous symbol is continuous, and invertibility gives Fredholmness at every level and smooth kernels and adjoint kernels. The kernels are independent of $s$, and smooth data in the range have smooth preimages. Smooth symbol paths admit norm-continuous quantizations; a path continuous in the classical symbol seminorms is continuous at every indicated operator norm.

If a compact Lie group $G$ acts smoothly on $X,E,F$, write $\rho_g(y):E_y\to E_{gy}$ for its bundle action and set $(U_gu)(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, with the analogous action on $F$. Invariant density and metrics can be chosen. Conjugation $P\mapsto U_gPU_g^{-1}$ is continuous in the classical symbol seminorms and in the displayed closures. Haar averaging commutes with the symbol map and preserves these classes, orders and smooth kernels. All assertions therefore apply to $G$-invariant operators, including $G=T\times O(k)$.

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $X$ a compact smooth $G$-manifold without boundary. A compact-support symbol triple on $T^*X$ consists of finite-rank continuous complex $G$-vector bundles $A,B$ and a continuous equivariant bundle map $b:A\to B$ which is an isomorphism off a compact subset. Triples are compared by equivariant bundle isomorphisms, block sum, continuous homotopies with a common compact support, and addition or removal of elementary triples whose map is everywhere invertible. These conventions concern actual bundle maps and their deformations; no previously defined equivariant $K$-group is assumed.

Write $R(G)$ for the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional continuous complex $G$-representations. For a smooth bundle map $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ on $T^*X\setminus0$, degree zero means $c(x,t\xi)=c(x,\xi)$ for all $t>0$, and elliptic means that $c(x,\xi)$ is a linear isomorphism for every $\xi\ne0$. For any other integer order $m$, homogeneous degree $m$ means $c(x,t\xi)=t^m c(x,\xi)$ for $t>0$. An order-zero realization is a classical order-zero operator, or a simultaneous-Sobolev-closure limit of such operators, whose degree-zero principal symbol is $c$. Its $L^2$ realization is a bounded map $P:L^2(X,E)\to L^2(X,F)$. For a bounded map $T:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H_1$ between Hilbert spaces, Fredholm means that $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, $\operatorname{ran}T$ is closed, and $\operatorname{coker}T:=\mathcal H_1/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite dimensional. The Hilbert adjoint $T^*$ then has kernel unitarily isomorphic to this cokernel. For an equivariant Fredholm realization define its index to be $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]\in R(G)$, using the induced finite-dimensional $G$-representations.

Every such triple has an index $a_G(A,B,b)\in R(G)$. It is realized as $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]$ by a $G$-invariant elliptic order-zero operator on smooth bundles over $X$. Its symbol is obtained by smoothing the triple, identifying its bundles with pullbacks from the zero section by radial transport, and replacing the invertible exterior symbol by a homogeneous degree-zero symbol. The index is independent of these operations, respects all the comparisons above and is additive under block sum. For a homogeneous elliptic symbol of any integer order, it equals the Fredholm index, in the same kernel-minus-adjoint-kernel convention, of every invariant classical or simultaneous-Sobolev-closure realization with that symbol.

The construction is natural under equivariant diffeomorphisms and restriction along homomorphisms between compact Lie groups. Tensoring all data by a finite-dimensional representation tensors the index by that representation. On a point it is the difference of the two fiber representations. Let $0\to C^\infty(X,E^0)\xrightarrow{d_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{d_{N-1}}C^\infty(X,E^N)\to0$ be a finite first-order differential complex, so $d_{j+1}d_j=0$, whose positive-frequency principal-symbol sequence is exact at every nonzero real cotangent vector. For a $G$-action by chain maps with section action $U_gu(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, put $H^j=\ker d_j/\operatorname{im}d_{j-1}$, with $d_{-1}=d_N=0$. Give the bundles invariant Hermitian metrics and a positive density, and let $d_{j-1}^*$ denote the formal adjoint. The harmonic subspace in degree $j$ is $\mathcal H^j=\{u\in C^\infty(X,E^j):d_ju=0,\ d_{j-1}^*u=0\}$, with the endpoint conditions interpreted using $d_{-1}=d_N=0$; a harmonic representative of a class in $H^j$ means its representative in $\mathcal H^j$. Its symbol index is $\sum_j(-1)^j[H^j]$; these cohomology representations are finite dimensional and every class has exactly one harmonic representative. This includes the de Rham complex.

Here is the controlled noncompact form. Let $U$ have an open equivariant embedding into a compact closed smooth $G$-manifold. For a compact-support triple on $T^*U$, its index can be computed after replacing it, through the same comparisons on a neighborhood of its support, by smooth base-bundle data $E,F$ and a homogeneous degree-zero symbol $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ for which $E=F=U\times V$ and $c=I_V$ outside a compact invariant subset of $U$, with $V$ a finite-dimensional representation. There is an elliptic invariant realization equal to the exterior bundle isomorphism off one compact invariant $L\subset U$, in both the source and target kernel variables; explicitly it has the form $P=\eta_2P_0\eta_1+h(1-\eta_1)$ with nested compactly supported cutoffs and exterior isomorphism $h$. Extending the bundles and this operator to any compact equivariant ambient manifold by the exterior trivializations gives the same virtual kernel representation. Thus the index is independent of that ambient embedding and satisfies excision for open equivariant inclusions whenever such compact ambients are supplied. No compactification of an arbitrary $G$-manifold is asserted.

Then $$K^0(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z[\beta]/(\beta^2),\qquad \widetilde K^0(S^2)=\mathbb Z\beta.$$ Restriction to a point is projection onto the integer summand. The sign of $\beta$ is tied to the stated clutching convention.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], all calculus and index constructions below use the declared AC hypothesis. The exponentials are an orthonormal complete system. Completeness can be checked without an additional spectral theorem: convolution of a continuous periodic function with the Fejér kernel is a trigonometric polynomial and converges uniformly, since the nonnegative kernel has integral one and its mass outside each neighborhood of zero tends to zero; continuous functions are dense in $L^2$ by approximation of interval indicators and simple functions. Thus an $L^2$ function orthogonal to every exponential is zero. Consequently $P_+$ is a norm-one orthogonal projection. On Fourier basis vectors, $A(e^{inx}v)=e^{i(n+1)x}v$ for $n\ge0$ and $A(e^{inx}v)=e^{inx}v$ for $n<0$. These images are exactly the distinct nonzero modes, so $A$ is an isometry onto their closed span, its kernel is zero, and its cokernel is the constants. Every identification commutes with $G$, proving $\operatorname{Ind}_G(A)=-[V]$.

To verify the actual classical symbol, let $f$ be a smooth cutoff supported in a coordinate interval of length less than $2\pi$, and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R$. With $\widehat f(\eta)=\int e^{-ix\eta}f(x)\,dx$, local application to $f(x)e^{ix\xi}$ gives $e^{-ix\xi}P_+(fe^{i(\cdot)\xi})(x)=(2\pi)^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}\widehat f(n-\xi)e^{ix(n-\xi)}$. Every derivative of $\widehat f$ decays faster than every power, by repeated integration by parts. For $\xi\to-\infty$ the sum and all its $x,\xi$ derivatives are rapidly decreasing, since $n-\xi\ge n+|\xi|$. For $\xi\to+\infty$ use full Fourier reconstruction, whose sum is $f(x)$ on the chosen chart, and subtract the sum over $n<0$; that sum has the same rapid estimates. Uniform bounds on the remaining compact $\xi$ interval follow by convergence of the differentiated sums. Hence this localized complete symbol has leading term $f(x)$ on the positive ray and zero on the negative ray, with smooth rapidly decreasing remainders away from a bounded frequency interval. Off the diagonal the localized kernels are smooth by the same integration-by-parts estimates. This establishes $P_+$ in the calculus [F1], with the asserted two-ray symbol. Multiplication by $e^{ix}$ gives the displayed elliptic symbol of $A$.

Choose a smooth real function $\varphi$ on $[0,2\pi]$, equal to $0$ near $0$, equal to $2\pi$ near $2\pi$, and increasing only in a proper interior interval $I$. The loops $u_t(x)=\exp(i((1-t)x+t\varphi(x)))$ are smooth periodic degree-one loops, for $0\le t\le1$, joining $e^{ix}$ to a loop equal to $1$ outside $I$. All derivatives match at the endpoints because $\varphi$ is constant there. On the positive cotangent ray replace $e^{ix}$ by $u_t(x)$, leaving the negative symbol $1$. These are elliptic symbol homotopies; [F2] preserves their index. At $t=1$ the symbol is the identity outside the compact subinterval where $\varphi$ varies, and its class is extended from $T^*I$. A coordinate on $I$ gives the following compact representative on $\mathbb R^2$: $a(x,\xi)=1+(e^{i\varphi(x)}-1)h(\xi)$, where $h=0$ on $\xi\le-1$, $h=1$ on $\xi\ge1$, and $\varphi$ is extended by its endpoint constants. Its possible zeros lie in a compact rectangle, and its boundary values are $e^{i\varphi(x)}$ on the top and $1$ on the other three sides.

Traverse that rectangle counterclockwise in the coordinate orientation $dx\wedge d\xi$. On the top $x$ decreases, so the change of argument is $-2\pi$. The boundary map has winding $-1$, whereas $x+i\xi$ has winding $+1$. Their class identity can also be seen directly: map the rectangle to a disk; the ratio of its boundary function to $\bar z$ has winding zero and hence a continuous logarithm (integrate its logarithmic derivative and use the zero total integral). Exponentiating scalar multiples of that logarithm gives a homotopy to $\bar z$. The sum of the $z$ and $\bar z$ relative symbols is zero: the boundary matrices $\operatorname{diag}(z,\bar z)$ contract through $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t z&-\sqrt{1-t^2}\\\sqrt{1-t^2}&t\bar z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $1\ge t\ge0$, to a constant invertible matrix, and then to the identity. Thus $[a]=-b$, consistently with [F3]. Tensoring the argument by $V$ proves the class assertion. Since $a$ has index $-[V]$ by steps 1.1 and 3.1, additivity and excision give $a_{\{1\}}(b)=1$, where $a$ denotes the compact-support analytic index. Finally $d\theta=d\xi\wedge dx$ reverses the chosen complex orientation, giving precisely the orientation statement in the example.
